q: Across the three walk-forward folds, is FOODS_1's forecast value add improving or deteriorating?
answer: Improving, monotonically across the three folds — but mostly because the baseline got worse, not because the model got better. FOODS_1 FVA: fold 1 (2013-05-05 to 2013-07-26) -16.3 pp, fold 2 (2013-07-27 to 2013-10-24) -8.4 pp, fold 3 (2013-10-25 to 2014-01-22) +4.3 pp, so it only clears the baseline in the final fold. Caveat: the model's own accuracy actually dipped in fold 3 (71.5% → 77.5% → 75.9%); the swing came from seasonal-naive accuracy collapsing from 87.8% to 85.9% to 71.6% as the holiday period made last-week repetition unreliable. Over the full 263 days FOODS_1 still has FVA of -7.3 pp and does not beat naive.

q: FOODS_1 loses to the naive baseline over the whole backtest — was that also true in December 2013?
answer: No — December 2013 is the one stretch where FOODS_1 beats the baseline. Over the full 263-day backtest FOODS_1 scores 75.0% forecast accuracy against 82.2% for seasonal-naive, an FVA of -7.3pp. In the 2013-12-01 to 2013-12-31 window the ranking flips: model 72.0% vs naive 61.8%, FVA +10.2pp. Note how it flips: the model didn't get better (72.0% in December is below its own 75.0% full-backtest accuracy) — the naive collapsed, from 82.2% to 61.8%, because holiday weeks break the same-weekday-last-week assumption. The clearest case is Christmas Day, 2013-12-25, when actual sales were 0 units: naive carried forward 436 units (absolute error 436) while the model's 298.6 was less wrong. The model still had bad December days of its own (2013-12-21: actual 625 vs model 298.6, error 326.4, worse than naive's 182.0), but on net the holiday disruption penalised the baseline more. So the full-backtest verdict stands in general; December is a holiday-driven exception, not evidence the model is stronger.

q: Is the model getting better over time?

output.note: volume_units is total units sold over the 263-day backtest window

answer:
No — if anything it's drifting worse. Scoped to the backtest window (2013-05-05 to 2014-01-22), measured two ways:

1) Weekly trend (pooled, all 7 departments): early weeks ran in the low-to-mid 80s (week of 2013-05-20: 86.4% forecast vs 89.2% naive), while the closing weeks are lower (2014-01-13: 76.0% vs 87.4% naive; 2014-01-20: 68.8% vs 89.9% naive). The naive baseline stays roughly flat in the mid-to-high 80s, so the gap widens rather than closes.

2) Walk-forward folds for the two biggest departments: FOODS_3 goes 81.8% → 80.4% → 78.2% across folds 1-3 (FVA -6.0pp → -7.7pp → -7.1pp), and HOUSEHOLD_1 goes 83.8% → 77.3% → 73.6% (FVA -5.0pp → -11.1pp → -12.3pp).

Context: pooled over the whole window the model is at 79.5% accuracy vs 85.2% for seasonal-naive (FVA -5.7pp), with only 2 of 7 departments beating the baseline. The one bright spot is the holiday stretch — weeks of 2013-12-02 (83.0% vs 72.7%) and 2013-12-30 (84.1% vs 73.9%) — where the model held up while the naive baseline broke down. Caveat: week-to-week accuracy is noisy, so read the fold numbers as the firmer evidence.

q: What caused the spike in FOODS_1 sales on December 21st 2013?
answer:
I can confirm the spike but not its cause — the backtest holds only actual/model/naive unit series, with no price, promotion, event, or weather fields, so causality is not answerable from this data.

What the data does show for FOODS_1 (CA_1): 2013-12-21 hit 625 actual units, the department's single largest error day (model 298.6, error 326.4 units; naive 443.0). It was the peak of a multi-day pre-Christmas run — 465 on 12-20, 571 on 12-22, 535 on 12-23, 486 on 12-24 — against a flat model forecast of 298.6 units/day. The store then recorded 0 units on 2013-12-25 (closure) and 179 on 12-26, with levels back near 300 by late December. So the shape is consistent with a holiday build-up, but that is an interpretation of the pattern, not a cause the tools can verify.
